defaults.permitted_development: Across Cornwall, the usual householder route for a driveway is strongest where the works stay within the plot and surface-water run-off is handled properly. Frontage parking areas over 5 square metres generally need permeable surfacing or drainage to a porous area, and a new vehicular crossing remains a separate highways matter.

rules.height_rules: Across Cornwall, a driveway does not have a simple national height limit, but raised platforms, retaining edges and stepped level changes can still turn a straightforward surfacing job into a planning issue.
rules.depth_rules: Across Cornwall, there is no fixed national depth limit, but the layout should leave enough space for vehicles to stand within the site instead of overhanging the footway. Front garden schemes are easiest to defend when drainage and manoeuvring have been solved together.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Cornwall, driveway works should stay within the curtilage, but widening an opening onto the road, crossing a verge or footway, or removing a front wall can trigger separate highway or planning issues. Visibility at the access often matters more than the paving choice on its own.
rules.roof_rules: Across Cornwall, a driveway does not trigger a roof test, but linked structures still matter. If you are adding a canopy or covered parking feature, it is not automatically covered by the surfacing rules.
rules.materials_rules: Across Cornwall, the easiest driveway material strategy is usually one that handles water on site rather than sending it to the road. Broad impermeable paving on a front garden is much more likely to create a planning issue than permeable or well-drained surfacing.

restrictions.conservation_area: Driveway works in conservation areas are usually judged as much on the loss of historic frontage character as on the paving material itself.
restrictions.listed_building: Driveway works affecting a listed building, its curtilage, or historic boundary structures can need listed building consent as well as any planning or highway approval.
restrictions.article4_notes: Driveway works are not always protected by normal householder rights: Article 4 controls and earlier planning conditions can require an application for surfacing or boundary changes.

rules.permitted_development: In Isles of Scilly, a driveway at a house is usually permitted development if it stays within the residential curtilage and, where it sits between the principal elevation and the highway, surfaces over 5 square metres are porous or drain to a permeable area within the plot. A new crossover or dropped kerb is a separate consent route and may still need highway approval or planning permission.

rules.height_rules: Height only becomes important on driveway schemes when the project relies on engineering works such as retaining walls, built-up levels or steep ramps. Those elements are often what move the proposal beyond the simplest householder route.
rules.depth_rules: There is no formula for driveway depth, but a shallow layout can still be refused in practice if it leaves vehicles hanging over the footway or creates poor manoeuvring and runoff problems.
rules.boundary_rules: A driveway is not only about the surface within the plot: the relationship with the road boundary, visibility splays and any altered opening can change the permission route altogether.
